steps.title: What the rule really says
steps.body: Rule (ii) compares the last digits $a\%10 \le b\%10$ and then recurses on $(\lfloor a/10\rfloor, \lfloor b/10\rfloor)$. It stops successfully only on $(0,0)$, so **every** digit position (padding the shorter number with leading 0s) must satisfy digit$(a) \le$ digit$(b)$.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body: Only (iii) and (iv) belong to P, which is option **D**.

it-2007-cs-24.approach: In a DAG there are no back edges, so every edge (u, v) is a tree, forward or cross edge; for all three, v finishes before u. Hence f[u] > f[v] always.

steps.title: Edge types in a DAG
steps.body: A back edge would close a cycle, so a DAG has only **tree, forward and cross** edges.

steps.title: Finish times for each type
steps.body:
- Tree/forward edge $(u,v)$: $v$ is a descendant of $u$, so $d[u] < d[v] < f[v] < f[u]$.
- Cross edge $(u,v)$: $v$ is already finished when $u$ looks at it, so $f[v] < d[u] < f[u]$.

In every case $f[u] > f[v]$ — this is exactly why sorting by decreasing finish time gives a topological order.

steps.title: Counter-examples for the rest
steps.body: Graph with edges $a\to b$ and $c\to b$, DFS started at $a$ first: $d[a]=1, d[b]=2, f[b]=3, f[a]=4, d[c]=5, f[c]=6$. For edge $(c,b)$: $d[c]=5 > d[b]=2$ (A fails), $d[c]=5 > f[b]=3$ (B fails), $f[c]=6 > f[b]=3$ (C fails).

optionAnalysis.reason: Fails for a cross edge: u can be discovered after v has been completely explored (d[c]=5 > d[b]=2 above).
Fails for a cross edge: v may already be finished before u is discovered (d[c]=5 > f[b]=3).
The reverse is true: v always finishes before u.
Correct: holds for tree, forward and cross edges, and a DAG has no back edges.

pitfalls: Assuming every edge is a tree edge — cross edges break d[u] < d[v].
it-2007-cs-24.verification: Checked all three possible edge types and built a concrete counter-example for A, B and C.

it-2007-cs-25.approach: A connected graph with n vertices and n edges is a spanning tree plus one extra edge, so it has exactly one cycle. Removing any one edge of that cycle gives a spanning tree, so the count equals the cycle length, which is at least 3 in a simple graph.

steps.title: Structure of the graph
steps.body: A spanning tree uses $n-1$ edges, so the graph has exactly $n-(n-1)=1$ extra edge, creating exactly **one cycle** of length $k$.

steps.title: Count spanning trees
steps.body: A spanning tree must drop exactly one edge, and it must be a cycle edge (dropping a non-cycle edge disconnects the graph). So there are exactly $k$ spanning trees.

steps.title: Minimise k
steps.body: In a simple graph (no loops or parallel edges) a cycle has $k \ge 3$, and $k=3$ is achievable (a triangle with a path hanging off it). Hence $m = 3$.

Would need a 2-cycle, i.e. parallel edges, which a simple graph cannot have.
Correct: the minimum cycle length 3 gives exactly 3 spanning trees, and no graph has fewer.
Only the n-cycle itself reaches n; a triangle with a pendant path has just 3.

pitfalls: Forgetting that the graph must be simple — with multi-edges the answer would be 2.
it-2007-cs-25.verification: n = 4 example: triangle {1,2,3} plus edge 3–4 has exactly 3 spanning trees (drop 1–2, 2–3 or 1–3).

it-2007-cs-26.approach: Use the exchange argument (Smith's rule): swapping two adjacent jobs changes only their own terms, and the swap helps exactly when the later job has the larger ratio w/t. So jobs must run in non-increasing order of w_i/t_i.

steps.title: Effect of swapping neighbours
steps.body:
The denominator $\sum w_i$ is fixed, so minimise $\sum w_iT_i$. Let $J_i$ and $J_j$ run back to back starting at time $s$:

$$i\text{ first: } w_i(s+t_i)+w_j(s+t_i+t_j)$$
$$j\text{ first: } w_j(s+t_j)+w_i(s+t_j+t_i)$$

Difference (i first − j first) $= w_jt_i - w_it_j$.

steps.title: Ordering rule
steps.body: $i$ first is no worse iff $w_jt_i \le w_it_j \iff \dfrac{w_i}{t_i} \ge \dfrac{w_j}{t_j}$. Any schedule violating this can be improved by a swap, so the optimum is **non-increasing order of $w_i/t_i$**.

steps.title: Check with an example
steps.body: $J_1$: $t=1, w=1$; $J_2$: $t=3, w=6$. Ratios 1 and 2. $J_2$ first: $6\cdot3 + 1\cdot4 = 22$; $J_1$ first: $1\cdot1+6\cdot4 = 25$. The higher ratio first wins, even though $J_1$ is shorter (A fails).

optionAnalysis.reason: Shortest-job-first ignores weights; in the example it gives 25 vs the optimal 22.
Ignores execution times: w=2, t=100 first gives 2·100 + 1·101 = 301, but the light short job first gives 1·1 + 2·101 = 203.
The product w·t rewards long jobs, the opposite of what is wanted.
Correct: the exchange argument shows the optimum is sorted by w/t in non-increasing order.

pitfalls: Minimising the unweighted mean (SJF) instead of the weighted one.
it-2007-cs-26.verification: Recomputed both orders for the two-job examples; the w/t ordering is always the cheaper one.

it-2007-cs-27.approach: Trace small values. Powers of two always terminate (infinitely many n), while n = 5 enters the cycle 5 → 14 → 7 → 20 → 10 → 5, and so does every 5·2^k (infinitely many n).

steps.title: A non-terminating value

Odd $n$ goes to $3n-1$:

$$5 \to 14 \to 7 \to 20 \to 10 \to 5 \to \cdots$$

The calls cycle forever, so $f(5)$ never terminates.

steps.body: For $n = 5\cdot 2^k$ the halving reaches 5 and enters the same cycle. So f fails to terminate for infinitely many $n$: (iv) true, (iii) false. Answer: (ii) and (iv).

(i) is false — every power of two terminates.
(iii) is false — 5·2^k loops forever for every k ≥ 0.

it-2007-cs-29.approach: On the search path to 60, keys smaller than 60 must appear in increasing order and keys larger than 60 in decreasing order (each step narrows the interval around 60). Only the interleaving of the two chains is free: C(7,3) = 35.

steps.title: Order within each side
steps.body: After visiting a key $x < 60$ the search goes right, so every later key is $> x$. Hence the smaller keys appear as $10, 20, 40, 50$ (increasing). Symmetrically, after $y > 60$ the search goes left, so the larger keys appear as $90, 80, 70$ (decreasing).

steps.body:
Both chains are forced; only their merge is free. Choose which 3 of the 7 positions hold the larger keys:

$$\binom{7}{3} = \frac{7\cdot6\cdot5}{3\cdot2\cdot1} = 35$$

animation.caption: Smaller keys increase, larger keys decrease; the two chains interleave freely.
